subsection: 3. The Germanic lands from Confederation to Empire, 1850–1871

notes.h: Background: the German Confederation and the failure of 1848–50
notes.b: To follow how the German lands reached empire in 1871, you need the starting point: a loose league of states, two rival great powers and a lesson learned from failure in 1848–50. Every later block builds on this.
points: The German Confederation, set up in 1815 at the Congress of Vienna, was a loose league of sovereign states with a Diet (an assembly of state delegates) at Frankfurt, presided over by Austria. Austria and Prussia were the two great powers in it, so their rivalry decided its future.

In 1849 Frederick William IV of Prussia refused the imperial crown offered by the Frankfurt Parliament (the elected assembly of 1848–49 that tried to unite Germany). Nationalists drew the lesson that unity would need Prussian power, not parliamentary votes.
The point to carry forward is that votes had failed and Prussian power was the alternative.

At the Punctation of Olmütz (November 1850) Prussia abandoned its Erfurt Union plan (a Prussian-led union of German states) under Austrian and Russian pressure. This humiliated Prussia; the Confederation and Diet were restored in 1851, and Bismarck became Prussia's delegate at the Diet that year.

The choice facing Germans was Kleindeutsch (a smaller Germany without Austria, under Prussia) or Grossdeutsch (a larger Germany including Austria). The events of 1866 settled the question in favour of Kleindeutsch.
notes.tip: Higher essays on this topic span 1815–1871. Open with a sentence or two on the 1815 Confederation and 1848–50, then spend most of the answer on 1862–71.

notes.h: Prussia's economic strength and Austria's weakness, 1850–1863
notes.b: After the failure of 1848, the balance between Prussia and Austria within the German Confederation turned on economic power and on the ability of each state to manage its own affairs. Prussia grew stronger and Austria weaker, which is why Prussia could later challenge it.
points: The Zollverein (the German customs union, in force from 1834 under Prussian leadership) included almost all German states except Austria by the 1850s; Hanover joined in 1854. It gave Prussia control of a large common market.
Tariff revenue was shared among Zollverein members, so the members were tied to Prussia economically.

The Ruhr (Rhineland-Westphalia) and Silesia, both Prussian, provided coal and iron. Rapid railway building from the 1840s linked the Prussian industrial regions to Berlin and to the Rhineland, so goods and, later, troops could move quickly.

Alfred Krupp's cast-steel works at Essen in the Ruhr, expanded rapidly from the 1850s, produced railway materials and steel guns. It symbolised Prussia's industrial power because it supplied both the railways and the army.

Prussia's 1862 commercial treaty with France, made for the Zollverein, lowered tariffs and set a low-tariff course. The other Zollverein states had accepted it by 1865, a course that Austria's protectionist system (high tariffs to shield its own industry) could not match.
Austria's finances were weak and its government remained centralised and conservative, with the Habsburg monarchy heavily in debt. This left it less able to modernise or to pay for a large army.
Austria's defeat in 1859 by France and Piedmont, at the battles of Magenta and Solferino, cost it Lombardy and exposed its military weakness.
Austria had alienated Russia by its hostile neutrality towards Russia in the Crimean War (1853–56), so it lacked a friend when Prussia challenged it.

Austria's attempt to reform the Confederation, the Frankfurt Princes' Congress (Fürstentag) of August 1863 called by Emperor Franz Joseph, collapsed because William I stayed away on Bismarck's advice. Without Prussia the plan could not work.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why Prussia beat Austria and why the Germanic lands moved to Empire. A clear thesis of Prussia's economic and military power plus Bismarck's diplomacy earns credit when you tie each stage to a specific event.

notes.h: Army reform and the constitutional crisis, 1858–1862
notes.b: Prussia's military strength was not automatic: it came from an army reform that provoked a fierce clash with the liberals in parliament. That clash is the setting in which Bismarck came to power.
points: William, the brother of Frederick William IV (who was incapacitated from 1857), became regent in 1858 and King William I in January 1861.
Roon's army reform kept three-year service, enlarged the regular army and reduced the role of the Landwehr (the citizen reserve militia). Liberals in the Landtag (the Prussian parliament) opposed it.
Albrecht von Roon, War Minister from 1859, organised the army, while Helmuth von Moltke, chief of the general staff from 1857, handled planning and command. Do not swap their roles.

The German Progressive Party (Fortschrittspartei) was founded in 1861. The liberal majority in the Prussian lower house refused to vote the army budget in 1862, so king and parliament were deadlocked.
The constitutional crisis deepened until William I considered abdicating and drew up an abdication document in September 1862.
In September 1862 William I appointed Otto von Bismarck Minister-President and Foreign Minister of Prussia to break the deadlock.
notes.tip: If asked about the September 1862 appointment, link it to the army-budget deadlock: Bismarck was chosen to break it. Do not confuse Roon (War Minister, army organisation) with Moltke (chief of the general staff).

notes.h: Bismarck in power: blood and iron and rule without a budget, 1862–1866
notes.b: Bismarck had to govern without the parliament's consent to the budget. He justified this with a legal argument and set out his view of how Germany would be united.
points: On 30 September 1862, in a speech to the Budget Committee of the Landtag, Bismarck said the great questions of the day would be decided not by speeches and majority decisions, the mistake of 1848 and 1849, but by "blood and iron".
By this he meant that force, not parliamentary debate, would settle German unity.
In the same speech he argued that Germany looked not to Prussia's liberalism but to its power. This told the liberals that he would use the army, not their ideas, to unite Germany.

Bismarck used the gap theory (Lückentheorie): the constitution did not say what happened if king and parliament disagreed, so the king's government could carry on. On this reasoning his government declared it was entitled to go on collecting taxes.
Taxes were collected and the army reform was carried out without an approved budget from 1862 to 1866. The conflict lasted until the Indemnity Bill of 1866.
notes.tip: Use only "blood and iron" in quotation marks for the 1862 speech and paraphrase the rest. Ordinary Level questions reward short dated facts: the September 1862 appointment, the army-budget deadlock, the blood and iron speech and ruling without a budget.

notes.b: The first of Bismarck's three wars showed his method: act with Austria against a weaker opponent, then use the settlement to prepare the quarrel with Austria itself.
points: Schleswig and Holstein (with Lauenburg) were ruled by the Danish king. Holstein was German-speaking and in the Confederation, while Schleswig was mixed Danish and German and outside it, and Germans wanted links with Germany.

Christian IX became King of Denmark in November 1863 and signed the November Constitution (1863), binding Schleswig to Denmark. This broke Danish undertakings of 1851–52 that were confirmed by the London Protocol of 1852, which also settled the Danish succession, and it provoked the German states.
Bismarck chose to act with Austria rather than alone so that the issue stayed a matter for the two great powers, not for the Diet or the liberals. It also kept a later quarrel with Austria available.
Prussia and Austria invaded Denmark jointly in February 1864. Prussia stormed Düppel (Dybbøl) in April 1864 and captured the island of Als in June 1864.
By the Treaty of Vienna (October 1864) Denmark ceded Schleswig, Holstein and Lauenburg to Prussia and Austria jointly. Their future was left to be settled between the two victors.

By the Convention of Gastein (August 1865) Austria administered Holstein and Prussia Schleswig, and Prussia bought Austria's rights in Lauenburg. This divided administration only, so it was a ready-made source of dispute and set up the conflict of 1866.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the 1864 Treaty of Vienna, which handed the duchies to both powers jointly, with the 1815 Congress of Vienna. Gastein (1865) divided only the administration, and for Ordinary Level it is the cause of the dispute with Austria.

notes.h: Isolating Austria and the road to war, 1863–1866
notes.b: Bismarck did not fight Austria until he had made sure it had no friends. Three separate diplomatic steps prepared the ground for war in 1866.
points: The Alvensleben Convention (February 1863) promised Prussian help to Russia against the Polish rising of 1863. Russian goodwill followed, which mattered because Austria had already lost Russian friendship in the Crimean War.
Bismarck met Napoleon III at Biarritz in October 1865, and Napoleon III remained neutral in the coming war. This freed Prussia from the risk of French intervention.
In April 1866 Prussia made an alliance with Italy that promised Venetia to Italy if Prussia won. Italy would attack Austria on a second front, so Austria faced war on two fronts.
In June 1866 Prussia declared the Gastein arrangements at an end and occupied Holstein. The Diet voted to mobilise against Prussia.

Most German states sided with Austria, including Bavaria, Saxony, Hanover, Württemberg and Hesse-Kassel. Prussia went to war against much of the Confederation, but its military and diplomatic advantages were greater.
notes.tip: Keep the three diplomatic steps separate: the Alvensleben Convention (1863, Russia), Biarritz (1865, France) and the Italian alliance (1866).

notes.h: The Austro-Prussian War and the Treaty of Prague, 1866
notes.b: The war was over in about seven weeks. Prussia's military superiority, not just its diplomacy, decided it, and Bismarck then chose a moderate peace to leave Austria a possible future friend.
points: Prussia won because of the Dreyse breech-loading needle-gun, which could be fired lying down and was faster than Austrian muzzle-loaders, and because of Moltke's planning. Moltke used railways to move armies quickly into Bohemia.

The battle of Königgrätz (also called Sadowa) in Bohemia, fought on 3 July 1866, was the decisive Prussian victory over the Austrian army under Benedek. The war lasted about seven weeks, which is why it is called the Seven Weeks' War.
Italy was beaten by Austria at Custoza (on land) and Lissa (at sea) in 1866 but still gained Venetia, thanks to Prussia's victory.

After Königgrätz, Bismarck persuaded William I and the generals to halt at the Nikolsburg preliminaries (July 1866), with no march on Vienna and no Austrian territory taken. His aim was to keep Austria as a future friend.

The Treaty of Prague (August 1866) dissolved the German Confederation and Austria accepted exclusion from German affairs. Venetia was ceded, via France, to Italy, and the Habsburg lands lay outside any German state.
Prussia annexed Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, Frankfurt and Schleswig-Holstein in 1866.
In August 1866 Bavaria, Württemberg and Baden signed secret offensive-defensive alliances with Prussia (each promising to fight alongside it if attacked), which tied the southern states to Prussia.
notes.tip: Königgrätz was decisive, but do not say it ended the war: the war ended with the Nikolsburg preliminaries (July) and the Treaty of Prague (August 1866). Do not confuse the Treaty of Prague (Prussia and Austria, 1866) with the Treaty of Frankfurt (1871).

notes.h: The Indemnity Bill and the split among the liberals, 1866–1867
notes.b: Victory in 1866 changed how Prussian liberals saw Bismarck. The question of the years without a budget had to be settled, and it divided them.
points: The Indemnity Bill, passed by the Prussian Landtag in September 1866, asked the Landtag to approve retrospectively the years of government without an approved budget. It gave Bismarck's rule a legal cover after the event.
The Bill split the liberals into those who gave way and those who stayed in opposition.

The National Liberal Party was founded in 1867 by liberals who backed Bismarck's national policy, so many liberals accepted his leadership in return for national unification. The remaining Progressives stayed in opposition.
notes.tip: Contemporary views of Bismarck changed over time: liberals were first hostile and then reconciled to him, as the Indemnity Bill and the National Liberal Party show.

notes.b: Prussia now had a framework to organise the north and to draw in the south. The Confederation was a step towards the Empire, built on Prussian dominance.
points: The North German Confederation was formed in 1867 by Prussia and the states north of the River Main, under Prussian leadership.

Its constitution, in force from 1 July 1867, made the King of Prussia president of the Confederation, with control of foreign policy and the armed forces. Bismarck was Federal Chancellor, so Prussia's king and minister ran the new union.

The Reichstag (the Confederation's parliament) was elected by universal manhood suffrage (every adult man could vote). The Bundesrat was made up of delegates of the state governments, and Prussia dominated it.

A Customs Parliament (Zollparlament) first met in 1868 with deputies from the southern states as well as the north. Southern voters returned many anti-Prussian (Catholic and particularist, meaning favouring each state's separate independence) deputies, so the south was not yet won.
notes.tip: Keep the North German Confederation (1867, north of the Main, Prussian-led) apart from the German Confederation (1815–66, Austrian-presided) and the Empire (1871). Also keep the Reichstag (elected), the Bundesrat (state governments) and the Prussian Landtag (three-class franchise) distinct.

notes.h: The road to the Franco-Prussian War: Luxembourg, Hohenzollern and Ems, 1867–1870
notes.b: France resented Prussia's rise, and Bismarck used a dispute over the Spanish throne to turn that resentment into a war in which France appeared the aggressor.
points: French resentment of Prussia's victory in 1866 was summed up as revenge for Sadowa. In the Luxembourg crisis of 1867 Napoleon III tried to buy Luxembourg from the King of the Netherlands; Prussian opposition stopped it, and the London Conference of 1867 made Luxembourg neutral.

In 1870 Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, from a Catholic branch of the Prussian royal family, accepted the Spanish crown, vacant since the 1868 revolution. This alarmed France, which feared encirclement by Hohenzollern rulers on two sides.
The withdrawal of Leopold's candidature was announced on 12 July 1870 after French pressure. France then demanded a guarantee that it would never be renewed.
On 13 July 1870 at Bad Ems the French ambassador Benedetti asked William I for that guarantee. William refused politely and had a report of the meeting telegraphed to Bismarck.
Bismarck shortened the report and released it to the press that evening. In its shortened form the Ems telegram made the exchange read as an insult to France.

France declared war on 19 July 1870 and appeared the aggressor. Bavaria, Württemberg and Baden joined Prussia under their treaties, while Austria, Italy and Britain stayed neutral and Russia was friendly to Prussia.
In July 1870 Bismarck published in The Times Benedetti's earlier draft treaty on French designs on Belgium, which turned British opinion against France. France was left with no ally.
notes.tip: Do not call the Ems telegram William's telegram: it was a report of the meeting telegraphed to Bismarck. Examiners reward Ems as an example of Bismarck's opportunism when you argue plan or opportunism.

notes.h: The Franco-Prussian War: Sedan and the fall of the Second Empire, 1870–1871
notes.b: Prussia's armies, with the southern states' troops beside them, won quickly. The war ended French resistance and removed Napoleon III.
points: Wörth and Spicheren (6 August 1870) were the first big French defeats. At Gravelotte–St Privat (18 August 1870) Prussia shut Bazaine's army in Metz.
Napoleon III had led the army to the front. At the battle of Sedan on 1 September 1870 the French were defeated, and Napoleon III and his army surrendered on 2 September 1870.

The Second Empire fell on 4 September 1870 when the Third Republic was proclaimed in Paris. Gambetta and the Government of National Defence carried on the war, and Gambetta left Paris by balloon to organise resistance in the provinces.
Bazaine surrendered Metz in October 1870. The siege of Paris lasted from September 1870 to January 1871, and the city capitulated in January 1871 and an armistice was signed on 28 January 1871.
Prussia won because of railways, superior artillery and Moltke's planning, together with the southern states' troops and France's isolation.
notes.tip: Get the Sedan dates right: the battle was on 1 September 1870 and the surrender on 2 September. For cause and result, name why Prussia beat France: planning, artillery, southern allies and French isolation.

notes.h: The proclamation of the German Empire and the Treaty of Frankfurt, 1870–1871
notes.b: Victory over France let Bismarck complete unification. He brought the southern states in by treaty and staged the proclamation in the palace of the defeated enemy.
points: In November 1870 treaties brought Baden, Hesse-Darmstadt (south of the Main), Württemberg and Bavaria into the union. Bavaria kept special rights: its own army in peacetime, post and railways.

In late 1870 King Ludwig II of Bavaria sent the Kaiserbrief, a letter drafted by Bismarck, asking William I to accept the title of emperor. This made the offer come from a southern prince, not from Prussia.

The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, with William I as German Emperor (Deutscher Kaiser). The date was the anniversary of the crowning of the first King in Prussia in 1701.
William was proclaimed at Versailles, in France, not in Berlin, and the title was German Emperor, not Emperor of Germany.

The Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871) ended the war. It transferred Alsace (except Belfort) and north-eastern Lorraine, including Metz, to Germany and required France to pay an indemnity of five billion francs, with German occupation until it was paid.
notes.tip: Learn the title (German Emperor) and the place (Versailles, 18 January 1871). Do not mix the Treaty of Frankfurt (1871, Germany and France) with the Frankfurt Parliament (1848–49) or the Frankfurt Diet.

notes.h: The constitution of the German Empire and its limits, 1871
notes.b: The Empire's constitution gave Germany a parliament but kept real power with the emperor and Prussia.
points: The imperial constitution of April 1871 was based on the 1867 constitution. It created a federal state of 25 member states plus the Reichsland of Alsace-Lorraine.
The King of Prussia was always German Emperor, so Prussian royal power and imperial power were joined in one person. The emperor controlled the army and foreign policy.

The Reichstag was elected by manhood suffrage, but the Chancellor was appointed by and answerable to the emperor alone, not to the Reichstag. This meant the elected house could not remove the head of government.
The Bundesrat, made up of the states' governments, gave Prussia 17 of 58 votes, and 14 votes could block a constitutional change. Prussia alone could therefore veto any amendment.

Prussia, with about two-thirds of the Empire's territory and about three-fifths of its population, kept its own three-class franchise, a voting system weighted towards the wealthy. This kept the dominant state conservative.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the achievements and limits of the 1871 settlement: unity achieved, but Prussian-dominated, with a weak Reichstag. Keep the Reichstag (elected, manhood suffrage), the Bundesrat (state governments) and the Prussian Landtag (three-class franchise) distinct.

notes.b: Bismarck was a Prussian conservative and Junker landowner who used war and diplomacy to create the German Empire. This part covers his role in unification.
points: Bismarck was born on 1 April 1815 at Schönhausen, in the Prussian province of Saxony, into a Junker (Prussian landowning noble) family. He sat in the United Diet of 1847 as an ultra-conservative and in the Prussian lower house from 1849.

He was Prussian delegate at the restored German Diet in Frankfurt from 1851 to 1859, which taught him to regard Austria as Prussia's rival. He was then ambassador at St Petersburg (1859–62) and at Paris (1862) before becoming Minister-President in September 1862.

As Minister-President he gave the "blood and iron" speech and used the gap theory to collect taxes and carry through the army reform without an approved budget. These steps gave him the means to build a strong army.

He was a participant who directed each stage of unification: the Danish War (1864), the Gastein settlement (1865), the alliance with Italy (1866), the war with Austria and the Treaty of Prague (1866), the North German Confederation (1867) and the Ems telegram (1870).
He became Chancellor of the North German Confederation in 1867 and Imperial Chancellor in 1871, holding office until 1890, and he was made a prince (Fürst) in 1871.

Contemporaries were divided: conservatives admired his success, while many liberals saw an authoritarian who had broken the constitution. Most liberals were won over by 1866–71, as the National Liberal Party shows.

Historians disagree. The Prussian school (for example Heinrich von Sybel and Heinrich von Treitschke) saw a master plan, and A. J. P. Taylor, in Bismarck: The Man and the Statesman (1955), portrayed an opportunist who improvised.

Lothar Gall's biography Bismarck: The White Revolutionary (German 1980) argued that he used revolutionary means, nationalism, manhood suffrage and war, to preserve the conservative order. The phrase had been used of Bismarck before Gall.
notes.tip: For personality essays, give concrete achievements (each war, each treaty, the 1867 and 1871 constitutions) and then a judgement on his contribution against the Prussian economic and military strength built before him. Do not credit Gall with inventing the phrase white revolutionary; say his biography called him that.

notes.b: Bismarck's aim was a Germany united under Prussian leadership. His methods were flexible, and historians argue about whether he followed a plan or seized chances.
points: Realpolitik, a term coined by Ludwig von Rochau in Principles of Realpolitik (1853), meant pursuing state interests through power and diplomacy rather than through principles or ideology. It was Rochau who coined it, not Bismarck.

Bismarck used liberal demands for national unity to win support for his policies, while keeping the army and the monarchy under royal control. In other words, he used liberal nationalism for Prussian ends.

He isolated each enemy before war: Russian goodwill after the Alvensleben Convention of 1863, Napoleon III's neutrality after Biarritz in 1865 and the alliance with Italy in 1866 against Austria, and France's lack of an ally in 1870.
He fought short wars with limited aims and avoided humiliating Austria in 1866, which made it easier for Austria to become a partner later.

He exploited chances as they arose: the Danish succession crisis, the Gastein arrangement, the Hohenzollern candidature and the Ems telegram, which created a public crisis that drew the southern states into the war.

The debate is whether he had a long-term plan to unite Germany under Prussia or exploited opportunities with a general aim of Prussian power. The Prussian school saw a plan, while Taylor saw an improviser.
The usual balanced verdict is a clear aim with flexible methods.
notes.tip: For plan or opportunism, name the historians (Taylor's opportunist, the Prussian school's master plan, Gall) and give a verdict of your own supported by events, such as Ems as opportunism and the isolation of Austria as design.

notes.b: Italy and Germany were unified in the same years, so examiners ask you to compare them. Both had a strong kingdom leading the way, but their paths and results differed.
points: Italy was unified between 1859 and 1871, with the Kingdom of Italy proclaimed in March 1861. Venetia was added in 1866 and Rome in September 1870, after the French garrison withdrew for the war with Prussia, and Rome became the capital from 1871.
Both unifications were led by a strong kingdom, Piedmont or Prussia, which combined war with diplomacy and treated Austria as the common enemy.
Italy won Venetia from Prussia's victory in 1866 even though Austria beat it at Custoza and Lissa. Rome was blocked until the French garrison left in 1870.
Piedmont needed French armies against Austria in 1859, whereas Prussia needed only foreign neutrality, so Prussia's military strength was far greater.
Italy's unity came partly from below, through Garibaldi's volunteers and plebiscites (votes by the people), while Germany's came from above, through the Prussian army and the princes.
Germany emerged far stronger economically and militarily than Italy.

Italy left Italian-speaking Trentino and Trieste in Austria, so unity was unfinished. Germany placed Danes in north Schleswig, Poles in Prussia's eastern provinces and Alsatians inside the Empire, and left out the Austrian Germans.
notes.tip: Examiners reward a judgement (Germany achieved greater unity and power) argued through paired similarities and differences, not two separate stories.

notes.h: Assessment: plan or opportunism, and the limits of the settlement
notes.b: The Empire was a real achievement but a limited one, and contemporaries and later historians judged it differently.
points: Achievement: unity, the aim of the liberals of 1848, was achieved by 1871 through Bismarck's wars and diplomacy.
Limit: unity came from above, by Prussian arms and the princes, not by a parliament, so it was not the liberal unity of 1848.
Limit: it was Kleindeutsch, leaving Austria, with its millions of Germans, outside the Empire. The Empire contained national minorities, Poles, Danes and, after 1871, Alsatians.

Limit: the Empire was a Prussian-dominated semi-autocracy (a system in which the ruler keeps most real power). The Reichstag, elected by manhood suffrage, had no control over the Chancellor and less power than the liberals had hoped.

Contemporary views: liberal supporters of unification saw the Empire as a national triumph (nationalism, the belief that a people sharing a language and culture should form one state, had been satisfied).
Later views: critics argued that the Empire was a Prussian-led autocracy built on militarism.
notes.tip: Give the 1871 settlement as paired points: unity achieved, but from above, Kleindeutsch, Prussian-dominated, with a weak Reichstag and minorities inside. Then set the liberals' view of a national triumph against later critics.

keyTerms.definition: Politics based on the pursuit of state interests through power and diplomacy rather than on principles or ideology, associated with Bismarck.
Bismarck's phrase from his 1862 speech to the Budget Committee, meaning that national questions would be decided by war and military strength rather than by majority votes.
The federation of north German states formed in 1867 under Prussian leadership, which was the basis for the German Empire.
The August 1866 treaty that ended the Austro-Prussian War, dissolved the German Confederation and excluded Austria from German affairs.
The telegram from King William I at Bad Ems, edited by Bismarck in July 1870, whose shortened version provoked France into war.
The elected lower house of the North German Confederation and the German Empire, chosen by universal male suffrage.
The upper house of the North German Confederation and the German Empire, made up of the governments of the member states and dominated by Prussia.
Rule by a single ruler with unlimited power; the Prussian-German system was a semi-autocracy in which the monarch, the army and a Chancellor answerable only to the emperor kept decisive power.
The belief that a people sharing language and culture should form a single state, which was the basis of the German unification movement.
The 1870 proposal of a Prussian prince for the Spanish throne, whose French opposition led to the Ems crisis and the Franco-Prussian War.

factCards.definition: Austria lost Lombardy after the Franco-Sardinian victories at Magenta and Solferino in 1859, which exposed its military weakness.
Austria's proposed reform of the German Confederation collapsed in 1863 because Prussia refused to attend.
Albrecht von Roon, War Minister from 1859, and Helmuth von Moltke, chief of the general staff from 1857, led the Prussian army reforms.
Prussian and Austrian forces defeated Denmark in these battles, and the Treaty of Vienna in October 1864 gave Schleswig and Holstein to the victors.
The arrangement that gave Austria the administration of Holstein and Prussia the administration of Schleswig, setting up the conflict of 1866.
The decisive Prussian victory over Austria, also called Sadowa, which ended the Austro-Prussian War.
Prussia annexed Hanover, Hesse-Kassel, Nassau, Frankfurt and Schleswig-Holstein after its victory over Austria.
In his speech to the Budget Committee Bismarck declared that the great questions of the day would be decided by blood and iron, not by majority votes.
William I was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 18 January 1871.
The treaty ended the Franco-Prussian War, transferred Alsace and part of Lorraine to Germany and imposed an indemnity of five billion francs on France.
The battle at which the French army was defeated and Napoleon III was captured, leading to the end of the Second Empire.
The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861, Venetia was added in 1866 after the alliance with Prussia, and Rome in 1870.
The Prussian school saw a master plan, A. J. P. Taylor an improvising opportunist, and Lothar Gall a white revolutionary.
It asked the Landtag to approve retrospectively Bismarck's years of rule without a budget, and it split the liberals.
